bib.title: A mathematical framework for learning probability distributions

bib.abstract:
Recent empirical studies have demonstrated that diffusion
models can effectively learn the image distribution and
generate new samples. Remarkably, these models can achieve
this even with a small number of training samples despite a
large image dimension, circumventing the curse of
dimensionality. In this work, we provide theoretical insights
into this phenomenon by leveraging key empirical
observations: (i) the low intrinsic dimensionality of image
data, (ii) a union of manifold structure of image data, and
(iii) the low-rank property of the denoising autoencoder in
trained diffusion models. These observations motivate us to
assume the underlying data distribution of image data as a
mixture of low-rank Gaussians and to parameterize the
denoising autoencoder as a low-rank model according to the
score function of the assumed distribution. With these
setups, we rigorously show that optimizing the training loss
of diffusion models is equivalent to solving the canonical
subspace clustering problem over the training samples. Based
on this equivalence, we further show that the minimal number
of samples required to learn the underlying distribution
scales linearly with the intrinsic dimensions under the above
data and model assumptions. This insight sheds light on why
diffusion models can break the curse of dimensionality and
exhibit the phase transition in learning distributions.
Moreover, we empirically establish a correspondence between
the subspaces and the semantic representations of image data,
facilitating image editing. We validate these results with
corroborated experimental results on both simulated
distributions and image datasets.

bib.abstract:
We give a new algorithm for learning mixtures of $k$
Gaussians (with identity covariance in $\mathbb{R}^n$) to TV
error $\varepsilon$, with quasi-polynomial ($O(n^{\text{poly
log}\left(\frac{n+k}{\varepsilon}\right)})$) time and sample
complexity, under a minimum weight assumption. Unlike
previous approaches, most of which are algebraic in nature,
our approach is analytic and relies on the framework of
diffusion models. Diffusion models are a modern paradigm for
generative modeling, which typically rely on learning the
score function (gradient log-pdf) along a process
transforming a pure noise distribution, in our case a
Gaussian, to the data distribution. Despite their dazzling
performance in tasks such as image generation, there are few
end-to-end theoretical guarantees that they can efficiently
learn nontrivial families of distributions; we give some of
the first such guarantees. We proceed by deriving
higher-order Gaussian noise sensitivity bounds for the score
functions for a Gaussian mixture to show that that they can
be inductively learned using piecewise polynomial regression
(up to poly-logarithmic degree), and combine this with known
convergence results for diffusion models. Our results extend
to continuous mixtures of Gaussians where the mixing
distribution is supported on a union of $k$ balls of constant
radius. In particular, this applies to the case of Gaussian
convolutions of distributions on low-dimensional manifolds,
or more generally sets with small covering number.

bib.abstract:
Diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art performance in various
generation tasks. However, their theoretical foundations fall far
behind. This paper studies score approximation, estimation, and
distribution recovery of diffusion models, when data are
supported on an unknown low-dimensional linear subspace. Our
result provides sample complexity bounds for distribution
estimation using diffusion models. We show that with a properly
chosen neural network architecture, the score function can be
both accurately approximated and efficiently estimated. Further,
the generated distribution based on the estimated score function
captures the data geometric structures and converges to a close
vicinity of the data distribution. The convergence rate depends
on subspace dimension, implying that diffusion models can
circumvent the curse of data ambient dimensionality.

bib.abstract:
We consider the problem of designing uniformly stable first-order
optimization algorithms for empirical risk minimization. Uniform
stability is often used to obtain generalization error bounds for
optimization algorithms, and we are interested in a general
approach to achieve it. For Euclidean geometry, we suggest a
black-box conversion which given a smooth optimization algorithm,
produces a uniformly stable version of the algorithm while
maintaining its convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. Using
this reduction we obtain a (nearly) optimal algorithm for smooth
optimization with convergence rate $\tildeO(1/T^2)$ and uniform
stability $O(T^2/n)$, resolving an open problem of Chen et al.
(2018); Attia and Koren (2021). For more general geometries, we
develop a variant of Mirror Descent for smooth optimization with
convergence rate $\tildeO(1/T)$ and uniform stability $O(T/n)$,
leaving open the question of devising a general conversion method
as in the Euclidean case.

bib.abstract:
We consider contractivity for diffusion semigroups w.r.t.
Kantorovich ($$L\textasciicircum1$$Wasserstein) distances based on
appropriately chosen concave functions. These distances are
inbetween total variation and usual Wasserstein distances. It is
shown that by appropriate explicit choices of the underlying
distance, contractivity with rates of close to optimal order can
be obtained in several fundamental classes of examples where
contractivity w.r.t. standard Wasserstein distances fails.
Applications include overdamped Langevin diffusions with locally
non-convex potentials, products of these processes, and systems of
weakly interacting diffusions, both of mean-field and nearest
neighbour type.

bib.abstract:
We investigate the problem of quantifying contraction
coefficients of Markov transition kernels in Kantorovich ($L^1$
Wasserstein) distances. For diffusion processes, relatively
precise quantitative bounds on contraction rates have recently
been derived by combining appropriate couplings with carefully
designed Kantorovich distances. In this paper, we partially carry
over this approach from diffusions to Markov chains. We derive
quantitative lower bounds on contraction rates for Markov chains
on general state spaces that are powerful if the dynamics is
dominated by small local moves. For Markov chains on $\mathbb
R^d$ with isotropic transition kernels, the general bounds can be
used efficiently together with a coupling that combines maximal
and reflection coupling. The results are applied to Euler
discretizations of stochastic differential equations with
non-globally contractive drifts, and to the Metropolis adjusted
Langevin algorithm for sampling from a class of probability
measures on high dimensional state spaces that are not globally
log-concave.

bib.abstract:
Score-based generative models (SGMs) have emerged as one of
the most popular classes of generative models. A substantial
body of work now exists on the analysis of SGMs, focusing
either on discretization aspects or on their statistical
performance. In the latter case, bounds have been derived,
under various metrics, between the true data distribution and
the distribution induced by the SGM, often demonstrating
polynomial convergence rates with respect to the number of
training samples. However, these approaches adopt a largely
approximation theory viewpoint, which tends to be overly
pessimistic and relatively coarse. In particular, they fail
to fully explain the empirical success of SGMs or capture the
role of the optimization algorithm used in practice to train
the score network. To support this observation, we first
present simple experiments illustrating the concrete impact
of optimization hyperparameters on the generalization ability
of the generated distribution. Then, this paper aims to
bridge this theoretical gap by providing the first
algorithmic- and data-dependent generalization analysis for
SGMs. In particular, we establish bounds that explicitly
account for the optimization dynamics of the learning
algorithm, offering new insights into the generalization
behavior of SGMs. Our theoretical findings are supported by
empirical results on several datasets.

bib.abstract:
Using continuous-time stochastic differential equation (SDE)
proxies to stochastic optimization algorithms has proven
fruitful for understanding their generalization abilities. A
significant part of these approaches are based on the
so-called ``entropy flows'', which greatly simplify the
generalization analysis. Unfortunately, such well-structured
entropy flows cannot be obtained for most discrete-time
algorithms, and the existing SDE approaches remain limited to
specific noise and algorithmic structures. We aim to
alleviate this issue by introducing a generic framework for
analyzing the generalization error of Markov algorithms
through `Poissonization', a continuous-time approximation of
discrete-time processes with formal approximation guarantees.
Through this approach, we first develop a novel entropy flow,
which directly leads to PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds.
We then draw novel links to modified versions of the
celebrated logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (LSI), identify
cases where such LSIs are satisfied, and obtain improved
bounds. Beyond its generality, our framework allows
exploiting specific properties of learning algorithms. In
particular, we incorporate the noise structure of different
algorithm types - namely, those with additional noise
injections (noisy) and those without (non-noisy) - through
various technical tools. This illustrates the capacity of our
methods to achieve known (yet, Poissonized) and new
generalization bounds.

George and Simsekli, Umut
bib.title:
Understanding the Generalization Error of Markov algorithms
through Poissonization

bib.abstract:
In statistical learning theory, generalization error is used to
quantify the degree to which a supervised machine learning
algorithm may overfit to training data. Recent work [Xu and
Raginsky (2017)] has established a bound on the generalization
error of empirical risk minimization based on the mutual
information I( S; W) between the algorithm input S and the
algorithm output W, when the loss function is sub-Gaussian. We
leverage these results to derive generalization error bounds for
a broad class of iterative algorithms that are characterized by
bounded, noisy updates with Markovian structure. Our bounds are
very general and are applicable to numerous settings of interest,
including stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) and
variants of the stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
(SGHMC) algorithm. Furthermore, our error bounds hold for any
output function computed over the path of iterates, including the
last iterate of the algorithm or the average of subsets of
iterates, and also allow for non-uniform sampling of data in
successive updates of the algorithm.

bib.abstract:
Modern machine learning usually involves predictors in the
overparameterised setting (number of trained parameters
greater than dataset size), and their training yields not
only good performance on training data, but also good
generalisation capacity. This phenomenon challenges many
theoretical results, and remains an open problem. To reach a
better understanding, we provide novel generalisation bounds
involving gradient terms. To do so, we combine the PAC-Bayes
toolbox with Poincaré and Log-Sobolev inequalities, avoiding
an explicit dependency on the dimension of the predictor
space. Our results highlight the positive influence of flat
minima (being minima with a neighbourhood nearly minimising
the learning problem as well) on generalisation performance,
involving directly the benefits of the optimisation phase.

bib.abstract:
We establish disintegrated PAC-Bayesian generalisation bounds
for models trained with gradient descent methods or
continuous gradient flows. Contrary to standard practice in
the PAC-Bayesian setting, our result applies to optimisation
algorithms that are deterministic, without requiring any
de-randomisation step. Our bounds are fully computable,
depending on the density of the initial distribution and the
Hessian of the training objective over the trajectory. We
show that our framework can be applied to a variety of
iterative optimisation algorithms, including stochastic
gradient descent (SGD), momentum-based schemes, and damped
Hamiltonian dynamics.

Generalisation under gradient descent via deterministic
{PAC}-Bayes

bib.abstract:
We develop a technique to test the hypothesis that multilayered,
feed-forward networks with few units on the first hidden layer
generalize better than networks with many units in the first
layer. Large networks are trained to perform a classification task
and the redundant units are removed (“pruning”) to produce the
smallest network capable of performing the task. A technique for
inserting layers where pruning has introduced linear
inseparability is also described. Two tests of ability to
generalize are used—the ability to classify training inputs
corrupted by noise and the ability to classify new patterns from
each class. The hypothesis is found to be false for networks
trained with noisy inputs. Pruning to the minimum number of units
in the first layer produces networks which correctly classify the
training set but generalize poorly compared with larger networks.

bib.title: Creating artificial neural networks that generalize

bib.abstract:
We study first-order algorithms that are uniformly stable for
empirical risk minimization (ERM) problems that are convex
and smooth with respect to $p$-norms, $p \geq 1$. We propose
a black-box reduction method that, by employing properties of
uniformly convex regularizers, turns an optimization
algorithm for Hölder smooth convex losses into a uniformly
stable learning algorithm with optimal statistical risk
bounds on the excess risk, up to a constant factor depending
on $p$. Achieving a black-box reduction for uniform stability
was posed as an open question by (Attia and Koren, 2022),
which had solved the Euclidean case $p=2$. We explore
applications that leverage non-Euclidean geometry in
addressing binary classification problems.
bib.author: Vary, Simon and Martínez-Rubio, David and Rebeschini, Patrick
bib.title:
Black-box uniform stability for non-Euclidean empirical risk
minimization

bib.abstract:
In recent years there has been increased interest in
understanding the interplay between deep generative models
(DGMs) and the manifold hypothesis. Research in this area
focuses on understanding the reasons why commonly-used DGMs
succeed or fail at learning distributions supported on
unknown low-dimensional manifolds, as well as developing new
models explicitly designed to account for manifold-supported
data. This manifold lens provides both clarity as to why some
DGMs (e.g. diffusion models and some generative adversarial
networks) empirically surpass others (e.g. likelihood-based
models such as variational autoencoders, normalizing flows,
or energy-based models) at sample generation, and guidance
for devising more performant DGMs. We carry out the first
survey of DGMs viewed through this lens, making two novel
contributions along the way. First, we formally establish
that numerical instability of likelihoods in high ambient
dimensions is unavoidable when modelling data with low
intrinsic dimension. We then show that DGMs on learned
representations of autoencoders can be interpreted as
approximately minimizing Wasserstein distance: this result,
which applies to latent diffusion models, helps justify their
outstanding empirical results. The manifold lens provides a
rich perspective from which to understand DGMs, and we aim to
make this perspective more accessible and widespread.
bib.author:
Loaiza-Ganem, Gabriel and Ross, Brendan Leigh and
Hosseinzadeh, Rasa and Caterini, Anthony L and Cresswell,
Jesse C
bib.title:
Deep generative models through the lens of the manifold
hypothesis: A survey and new connections

bib.abstract:
The denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) has
emerged as a mainstream generative model in generative AI.
While sharp convergence guarantees have been established for
the DDPM, the iteration complexity is, in general,
proportional to the ambient data dimension, resulting in
overly conservative theory that fails to explain its
practical efficiency. This has motivated the recent work Li
and Yan (2024a) to investigate how the DDPM can achieve
sampling speed-ups through automatic exploitation of
intrinsic low dimensionality of data. We strengthen this line
of work by demonstrating, in some sense, optimal adaptivity
to unknown low dimensionality. For a broad class of data
distributions with intrinsic dimension $k$, we prove that the
iteration complexity of the DDPM scales nearly linearly with
$k$, which is optimal when using KL divergence to measure
distributional discrepancy. Notably, our work is closely
aligned with the independent concurrent work Potaptchik et
al. (2024) -- posted two weeks prior to ours -- in
establishing nearly linear-$k$ convergence guarantees for the
DDPM.
bib.author: Huang, Zhihan and Wei, Yuting and Chen, Yuxin
bib.title:
Denoising diffusion probabilistic models are optimally
adaptive to unknown low dimensionality

bib.abstract:
This paper presents a dimension-free Harnack type inequality for
heat semigroups on manifolds, from which a dimension-free lower
bound is obtained for the logarithmic Sobolev constant on compact
manifolds and a new criterion is proved for the logarithmic
Sobolev inequalities (abbrev. LSI) on noncompact manifolds. As a
result, it is shown that LSI may hold even though the curvature of
the operator is negative everywhere.
bib.author: Wang, Feng-Yu
bib.title:
Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities on noncompact Riemannian

bib.abstract:
We obtain the first analytic, interpretable and predictive
theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models.
Indeed, score-based diffusion models can generate highly
creative images that lie far from their training data. But
optimal score-matching theory suggests that these models
should only be able to produce memorized training examples.
To reconcile this theory-experiment gap, we identify two
simple inductive biases, locality and equivariance, that: (1)
induce a form of combinatorial creativity by preventing
optimal score-matching; (2) result in a fully analytic,
completely mechanistically interpretable, equivariant local
score (ELS) machine that, (3) without any training can
quantitatively predict the outputs of trained convolution
only diffusion models (like ResNets and UNets) with high
accuracy (median $r^2$ of $0.90, 0.91, 0.94$ on CIFAR10,
FashionMNIST, and MNIST). Our ELS machine reveals a locally
consistent patch mosaic model of creativity, in which
diffusion models create exponentially many novel images by
mixing and matching different local training set patches in
different image locations. Our theory also partially predicts
the outputs of pre-trained self-attention enabled UNets
(median $r^2 \sim 0.75$ on CIFAR10), revealing an intriguing
role for attention in carving out semantic coherence from
local patch mosaics.
bib.author: Kamb, Mason and Ganguli, Surya
bib.title:
An analytic theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion
models

bib.abstract:
Score-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art
sampling performance by denoising a distribution perturbed by
Gaussian noise. In this paper, we focus on a single
deterministic denoising step, and compare the optimal
denoiser for the quadratic loss, we name ''full-denoising'',
to the alternative ''half-denoising'' introduced by Hyvärinen
(2024). We show that looking at the performances in term of
distance between distribution tells a more nuanced story,
with different assumptions on the data leading to very
different conclusions. We prove that half-denoising is better
than full-denoising for regular enough densities, while
full-denoising is better for singular densities such as
mixtures of Dirac measures or densities supported on a
low-dimensional subspace. In the latter case, we prove that
full-denoising can alleviate the curse of dimensionality
under a linear manifold hypothesis.
bib.author: Beyler, Eliot and Bach, Francis
bib.title:
Optimal denoising in score-based generative models: The role
of data regularity

title: Predicting Air Pollution in Cork, Ireland Using Machine Learning
summary:
Air pollution poses a critical health threat in cities worldwide, with
nitrogen dioxide levels in Cork, Ireland exceeding World Health Organization
safety standards by up to $278\%$. This study leverages artificial intelligence
to predict air pollution with unprecedented accuracy, analyzing nearly ten
years of data from five monitoring stations combined with 30 years of weather
records. We evaluated 17 machine learning algorithms, with Extra Trees emerging
as the optimal solution, achieving $77\%$ prediction accuracy and significantly
outperforming traditional forecasting methods. Our analysis reveals that

seasonal changes create predictable pollution cycles. Pollution exhibits
dramatic seasonal variations, with winter levels nearly double those of summer,
and daily rush-hour peaks reaching $120\%$ above normal levels. While Cork's

demonstrates that intelligent forecasting systems can provide city planners and

exists today to transform urban air quality management. All research materials
and code are freely available at:

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Urban air pollution represents one of the most pressing environmental challenges of the 21st century, affecting billions of people worldwide and imposing substantial burdens on public health, environmental systems, and economic development \cite{who2021guidelines}. Among the various atmospheric pollutants, nitrogen dioxide (NO\textsubscript{2}) has emerged as a critical indicator of urban air quality due to its direct health impacts and role as a precursor to secondary pollutant formation \cite{zhang2022forecasting}. The World Health Organization recognizes NO\textsubscript{2} as a primary concern for respiratory health, particularly affecting vulnerable populations including children, elderly individuals, and those with pre-existing respiratory conditions \cite{who2021guidelines,liu2021spatiotemporal}. Cork, Ireland's second-largest city, exemplifies the contemporary urban air quality challenges facing medium-sized European cities, with its expanding urban population, increasing vehicular traffic, and evolving industrial landscape contributing to episodic air pollution events that frequently exceed international health guidelines. The city's unique geographical setting, characterized by its coastal location and complex topography, creates distinctive meteorological conditions that significantly influence pollutant dispersion and accumulation patterns. The complexity of urban air quality systems stems from the multifaceted nature of pollution sources and the dynamic interplay of meteorological factors that govern pollutant transport, transformation, and removal processes. Traditional statistical approaches have proven inadequate for capturing the non-linear, temporal, and spatially heterogeneous characteristics of urban atmospheric systems \cite{feng2023hybrid,li2024deep}, consequently highlighting the need for advanced computational methodologies that can effectively model these complex environmental systems.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=13cm, height=9cm]{Images/Cork_Air_Quality_Overview.png}
\caption{Overview of the Cork Air Quality Monitoring Network and Research Framework: Five strategically positioned monitoring stations across Cork, Ireland, providing comprehensive NO\textsubscript{2} measurements integrated with meteorological data from Cork Airport, enabling machine learning-based prediction of urban air pollution patterns.}
\label{fig:cork_overview}
\end{figure}

Recent technological advances in environmental monitoring have generated unprecedented volumes of high-resolution air quality and meteorological data, with Cork's comprehensive air quality measurements from five strategically positioned monitoring stations, combined with extensive meteorological observations spanning three decades, providing an exceptional foundation for advanced atmospheric modeling \cite{huang2023ensemble}. However, the integration and analysis of these multi-source, multi-temporal datasets present significant methodological challenges, requiring sophisticated data processing techniques and robust analytical frameworks. Machine learning approaches have emerged as powerful tools for environmental prediction, offering the capability to model complex non-linear relationships, capture temporal dependencies, and handle large-scale datasets effectively \cite{mendez2023machine}. Advanced algorithms such as Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost have demonstrated particular promise in atmospheric applications due to their ability to handle mixed data types, manage outliers, and capture complex interaction effects \cite{zaini2022pm25,guo2023prediction}, with these ensemble methods leveraging the collective intelligence of multiple models to improve prediction accuracy and robustness compared to individual algorithms. Despite these technological advances, significant research gaps remain in the application of machine learning to urban air quality prediction, as most existing studies focus on short-term forecasting or single-pollutant models, with limited consideration of the comprehensive meteorological drivers that influence urban atmospheric conditions \cite{kostadinov2024forecasting}. Furthermore, few studies have systematically evaluated the performance of diverse machine learning algorithms across multiple monitoring locations within a single urban area, limiting our understanding of algorithm suitability for different environmental contexts.


The primary objective of this research is to develop and evaluate a comprehensive machine learning framework for NO\textsubscript{2} concentration prediction in Cork, Ireland, utilizing extensive air quality and meteorological datasets, with specific aims including: (1) systematic evaluation of seventeen different machine learning algorithms to identify optimal approaches for urban air quality prediction; (2) comprehensive analysis of meteorological and temporal factors influencing NO\textsubscript{2} concentrations; (3) development of advanced feature engineering techniques to enhance model predictive capability; and (4) assessment of model performance across multiple monitoring locations to evaluate transferability and robustness. Through systematic evaluation of seventeen machine learning algorithms, this research demonstrates that ensemble methods, particularly the Extra Trees algorithm, achieve superior performance for urban NO\textsubscript{2} prediction with an R² of 0.7724, significantly outperforming traditional statistical approaches and individual machine learning models. The study reveals that bagging ensemble methods consistently outperform boosting algorithms in atmospheric prediction applications, with Random Forest achieving R² of 0.7337, Bagging RF reaching R² of 0.6962, and XGBoost obtaining R² of 0.6628, while key meteorological variables such as temperature, wind speed, and humidity serve as the most influential predictors alongside temporal features reflecting human activity patterns. This research contributes to the scientific understanding of urban air quality systems through several key innovations. First, it provides the most comprehensive comparative evaluation of machine learning algorithms for urban air quality prediction conducted to date, establishing Extra Trees as the optimal algorithm with superior generalization capability (see Section~\ref{subsec:results_performance} and Table~\ref{tab:model_performance_combined}). Second, the study introduces novel feature engineering approaches, including wind-adjusted concentration metrics and comprehensive lag variable implementation, that enhance model interpretability and predictive performance (detailed in Section~\ref{subsec:data_preparation} and Section~\ref{subsec:exploratory_analysis}). Third, the research demonstrates the practical application of advanced ensemble learning techniques for regulatory compliance assessment and early warning system development (outlined in Section~\ref{subsec:regulatory_benchmarking} and Section~\ref{subsec:results_performance}). Finally, the findings provide evidence-based recommendations for environmental management authorities and urban planners seeking to implement predictive air quality systems for public health protection and sustainable urban development (discussed in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).


\section{Literature Review}
\label{sec:literature_review}

\textbf{Evolution of Air Quality Prediction Methods} Air quality forecasting has undergone significant methodological evolution, transitioning from traditional statistical approaches to sophisticated machine learning and deep learning frameworks. Early research relied heavily on linear regression models and time series analysis, particularly ARIMA methods, which provided foundational understanding but struggled with the non-linear and complex relationships inherent in atmospheric systems \cite{kaur2023autoregressive}. The introduction of machine learning techniques marked a paradigm shift, offering enhanced capability to capture complex patterns and relationships in environmental data. Statistical approaches, while maintaining importance for baseline comparisons, have been increasingly supplemented by ensemble methods and neural network architectures that can better handle the multidimensional nature of air quality prediction challenges.

\textbf{Machine Learning and Ensemble Methods in Air Quality Prediction} Contemporary research has demonstrated the superiority of ensemble learning approaches over individual algorithms for air quality prediction applications. Advanced ensemble techniques have shown remarkable success across diverse geographic contexts, with studies demonstrating the effectiveness of combining multiple algorithms to improve prediction accuracy and robustness \cite{huang2023ensemble}. Tao et al. (2024) presented a comprehensive ensemble model combining Transformer, XGBoost, and GRU networks for NO\textsubscript{2} predictions in China, achieving substantial improvements in prediction accuracy through strategic algorithm integration \cite{tao2024time}. Similarly, ensemble-imputation-classification frameworks have been developed to address the persistent challenge of missing values in air quality datasets, demonstrating improved data handling capabilities compared to traditional imputation methods \cite{narasimhan2023machine}. The success of these ensemble approaches stems from their ability to leverage the strengths of multiple algorithms while compensating for individual model limitations, particularly important in atmospheric prediction where different algorithms may excel under varying meteorological conditions.

Tree-based ensemble methods, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost, have emerged as particularly effective for environmental applications due to their inherent ability to handle mixed data types, manage outliers, and capture complex interaction effects without extensive preprocessing requirements \cite{zaini2022pm25,guo2023prediction}. These algorithms have demonstrated consistent performance across diverse urban environments, from hyperparameter optimization approaches for PM\textsubscript{2.5} prediction in Istanbul \cite{erden2023genetic} to integrated Air Quality Index modeling frameworks \cite{wang2023combined}. The robustness of tree-based methods extends to their capacity for handling temporal dependencies and non-linear relationships, making them particularly suitable for atmospheric modeling applications where pollutant concentrations exhibit complex response patterns to meteorological variables.

\textbf{Deep Learning and Neural Network Approaches} The application of deep learning techniques to air quality prediction has introduced novel capabilities for spatial-temporal modeling and uncertainty quantification. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained prominence through innovations such as Self-Supervised Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks for city-wide air quality predictions, offering sophisticated approaches to capture spatial dependencies across monitoring networks \cite{han2023semi}. Advanced neural architectures, including lightweight sparse attention-based Transformer networks and ResNet-ConvLSTM combinations, have demonstrated effectiveness for PM\textsubscript{2.5} prediction across diverse geographic contexts from China \cite{zhang2023modeling} to Saudi Arabia \cite{elbaz2023spatiotemporal}. Convolutional neural networks have shown particular promise for high-resolution temporal prediction, with CNN-based hourly PM\textsubscript{2.5} forecasting systems demonstrating operational capability in challenging environments such as Tripoli, Libya \cite{esager2023forecasting}.

However, deep learning approaches present unique challenges, particularly regarding uncertainty quantification and interpretability. Recognizing these limitations, researchers have developed probabilistic forecasting approaches using Bayesian deep learning frameworks for real-time applications \cite{abirami2023probabilistic}, while interpretable variational Bayesian deep learning models have been proposed to address the critical need for model transparency in environmental prediction \cite{jin2023variational}. The integration of traditional signal processing techniques with deep learning architectures, such as CART feature selection combined with TVF-EMD and ensemble DRVFL, has shown promise for addressing the complexity of atmospheric time series while maintaining computational efficiency \cite{jamei2023multi}.

\textbf{Geographic Diversity and Methodological Challenges} Recent literature demonstrates significant geographic diversity in air quality prediction research, with studies spanning Asian megacities, European urban centers, Middle Eastern developments, and North American regions. This geographic breadth has revealed the importance of region-specific modeling approaches, as atmospheric dynamics, emission patterns, and meteorological influences vary substantially across different climate zones and urban configurations. Multi-step multi-output multivariate models have been developed to address the challenge of predicting multiple air pollutants simultaneously, as demonstrated in Ho Chi Minh City applications \cite{rakholia2023multi}, while specialized approaches have emerged for addressing regional challenges such as wildfire impacts in the Pacific Northwest \cite{fan2023machine} and COVID-19 lockdown effects on air quality in India \cite{singh2023analysis}.

The methodological challenges identified across these diverse applications include data quality issues, temporal resolution optimization, and the integration of heterogeneous data sources. Advanced preprocessing techniques have become increasingly sophisticated, with data assimilation methods integrated with machine learning for emission adjustment in Community Multiscale Air Quality modeling systems \cite{huang2023data}. Novel approaches such as enhanced Markov chain synergies with clustering techniques have been developed to address the complexity of spatiotemporal air quality data \cite{yan2023improved}, while comprehensive frameworks for Air Quality Index prediction have incorporated multiple temporal scales and uncertainty quantification \cite{zhan2023probabilistic}.

\textbf{Research Gaps and Future Directions} Despite significant advances in air quality prediction methodologies, several critical research gaps remain. Most existing studies focus on short-term forecasting horizons, with limited investigation of long-term prediction capability and seasonal pattern modeling. The systematic evaluation of algorithm performance across multiple urban environments remains limited, constraining our understanding of model transferability and generalization capability. Furthermore, few studies have comprehensively addressed the integration of meteorological forecasting uncertainty into air quality prediction frameworks, potentially limiting operational forecasting accuracy. The development of hybrid approaches that combine the interpretability of traditional methods with the predictive power of advanced machine learning techniques represents an emerging research frontier, particularly important for regulatory applications where model transparency is essential for policy implementation and public communication.


\section{Materials and Methods}
\label{sec:materials_methods}

\subsection{Study Area and Data Sources}
\label{subsec:study_area}


Temporal coverage spans June 2020 to June 2023 across all locations of Cork, Ireland, with extended historical data (2014-2018) for South Link Road, complemented by meteorological observations from Cork Airport's Met Éireann station (1993-2023) located 6 kilometers south, encompassing temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind characteristics, precipitation, solar radiation, visibility, and cloud cover parameters. Integration of these multi-source datasets resulted in 56,708 observations across 14 variables, detailed in Table \ref{tab:stats}, which presents Cork Air Quality descriptive statistics serving as the primary modeling focus due to extended temporal coverage, revealing substantial NO\textsubscript{2} variability (mean 21.10 $\mu$g/m³, standard deviation 18.64 $\mu$g/m³, range from 0 to 407.81 $\mu$g/m³ peaks), temperate oceanic climate conditions with temperature averaging 10.22°C (-6.9°C to 27.8°C), moderate wind speeds (mean 9.66 m/s) with predominant southwesterly directions (211°) consistent with Atlantic weather systems, high relative humidity (mean 85.97\%) reflecting maritime influence, and atmospheric pressure variations (951.5 to 1047.2 hPa) indicating diverse weather system passage.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering

\label{subsec:data_preparation}

Data preparation followed a systematic three-stage approach encompassing duplicate removal, outlier detection, and negative value treatment to ensure data integrity across 56,708 observations. The preprocessing pipeline first eliminated duplicate records through automated temporal stamp validation, excluded irrelevant variables (O\textsubscript{3}, PM\textsubscript{10}), and decomposed date-time variables into constituent components (year, month, day, hour) for temporal pattern analysis, as illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:data_cleaning}.

Outlier detection was implemented using the Interquartile Range (IQR) method, flagging observations falling outside the Q1–1.5×IQR and Q3+1.5×IQR thresholds for each variable. Table~\ref{tab:outliers} presents the number of detected outliers before and after applying a multi-criteria assessment framework that combined statistical thresholds with physical plausibility checks. NO\textsubscript{2} exhibited the highest prevalence of outliers, with 2,287 flagged and 2,187 retained after plausibility screening, resulting in a net reduction of 100 values (4.37\%). Similarly, relative humidity, mean sea-level pressure, and temperature underwent selective outlier removal based on expert judgment, leading to total reductions of 5.19\%, 5.15\%, and 4.02\% respectively. In total, approximately 1.1\% of all observations were removed, balancing statistical rigor with the need to preserve valid atmospheric patterns and avoid overcleaning.

Negative NO\textsubscript{2} values, which are physically implausible under standard atmospheric conditions, were systematically addressed through a data-driven thresholding process grounded in both statistical evidence and domain expertise. Figure~\ref{fig:negative_threshold} illustrates the kernel density estimation (KDE) of the negative NO\textsubscript{2} values, revealing a distribution heavily concentrated near zero with a long tail extending toward more extreme negative values. The analysis identified 981 negative NO\textsubscript{2} values (1.45\% of the dataset), ranging from -51.10 to -0.01~$\mu$g/m³, with a mean of -2.29~$\mu$g/m³. To establish a statistically robust threshold, the 5\textsuperscript{th} percentile of negative values was calculated at -8.47~$\mu$g/m³. This threshold represents the boundary between measurement noise and likely sensor malfunctions, as values below this threshold are statistically rare and more likely to represent instrument errors or data corruption. The cleaning strategy employed a two-tier approach: (1) Values below the -8.47~$\mu$g/m³ threshold (representing 10,738 observations) were completely removed from the dataset as they likely indicate sensor malfunctions, calibration errors, or data corruption events. (2) Values between the threshold (-8.47~$\mu$g/m³) and zero (932 observations) were converted to zero, interpreting them as minor measurement noise, rounding artifacts, or values near the detection limit that should be treated as background levels.
This approach balances statistical rigor with physical plausibility, ensuring that the cleaned dataset maintains data integrity while removing clearly erroneous measurements. The resulting dataset contained 56,708 observations with NO\textsubscript{2} values ranging from 0 to 407.81~$\mu$g/m³, providing a robust foundation for machine learning analysis without introducing artifacts from negative measurements.

\section{Experiment}
\label{sec:experiment}

\subsection{Experimental Design and Implementation}
\label{subsec:experimental_design}

The experimental framework was designed as a comprehensive, reproducible pipeline for urban air quality prediction, implementing 17 distinct machine learning algorithms with systematic evaluation protocols. The experimental design follows a sequential five-stage approach: (1) data preprocessing and feature engineering, (2) model portfolio creation and configuration, (3) systematic training and evaluation pipeline, (4) performance assessment and ranking, and (5) visualization and documentation generation. The implementation employs Python 3.8+ with essential libraries including scikit-learn 1.3+, pandas 1.5+, numpy 1.24+, matplotlib 3.6+, and specialized packages (XGBoost 1.7+, CatBoost 1.2+, LightGBM 3.3+) for advanced ensemble methods. The experimental constants include random\_state=42 for reproducibility, 80/20 train-test split ratio, and StandardScaler normalization with Z-score transformation. Directory structure management creates separate folders for trained models (trained\_models/), experimental tables (experimental\_results\_tables/), and visualization outputs (visualization\_results/), enabling organized result storage and analysis.

\subsection{Model Portfolio and Training Pipeline}
\label{subsec:model_portfolio}

The model portfolio encompasses 17 algorithms strategically selected to capture diverse learning paradigms and atmospheric data characteristics. \textbf{Base Models (14)} include Linear Regression for baseline comparison, regularized methods (Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet) with L1/L2 penalties, tree-based algorithms (Decision Tree, Random Forest) for non-linear patterns, boosting ensembles (XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost) for sequential error reduction, distance-based methods (K-Nearest Neighbors) for local pattern recognition, Support Vector Regression with RBF kernel for complex boundary modeling, and Multi-Layer Perceptron for neural network representation. \textbf{Advanced Ensemble Models (3)} include Extra Trees Regressor with randomized feature selection, Bagging Random Forest for variance reduction, and Voting Regressor combining Random Forest, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting through hard voting. The training pipeline implements systematic data preprocessing. Date feature extraction decomposes timestamps into Year, Month, Day, Hour components, while seasonal encoding transforms categorical Season variables using Label Encoder. Missing value handling employs listwise deletion for NO\textsubscript{2} target variables, maintaining data integrity while preserving sample size. Feature scaling applies StandardScaler with Z-score normalization ($z_i = (x_i - \mu) / \sigma$) to ensure equal weighting across variables with different measurement scales. The train\_test\_split function implements 80/20 data partitioning with random\_state=42, creating training sets (45,366 samples) and testing sets (11,342 samples) while preserving temporal and spatial distribution characteristics.

\subsection{Evaluation Protocol and Performance Metrics}
\label{subsec:evaluation_protocol}

The evaluation protocol implements comprehensive multi-metric assessment, calculating five complementary performance indicators for both training and testing datasets. \textbf{Primary Metrics} include Mean Absolute Error ($MAE$) for interpretable error magnitude, Root Mean Squared Error ($RMSE$) for penalizing large deviations, and R-squared coefficient ($R^2$) for variance explanation assessment. \textbf{Supplementary Metrics} include Mean Squared Error (MSE = RMSE²) for mathematical completeness and Mean Absolute Percentage Error ($MAPE$) for scale-independent comparison, with adjusted R-squared calculation accounting for feature dimensionality effects. \textbf{Overfitting Detection} employs systematic comparison between training and testing R² scores, identifying models with substantial performance degradation ( $> 0.2$ R² difference) as potentially overfitted. Model persistence utilizes joblib serialization for reproducible deployment, while performance tracking stores comprehensive results in structured CSV formats. The evaluation framework ensures fair comparison through consistent random state settings and identical preprocessing steps across all algorithms. \textbf{Ranking and Selection} automatically identifies optimal models based on testing R² scores, with comprehensive performance summaries enabling detailed model comparison and selection for specific deployment scenarios.

\subsection{Results and Model Performance Analysis}
\label{subsec:results_performance}

The comprehensive experimental evaluation of 17 machine learning algorithms, 11 deep learning models, and 5 traditional time series models revealed significant insights into urban air quality prediction capabilities, with distinct performance patterns emerging across different algorithmic approaches and environmental contexts. This analysis encompasses algorithm-specific performance assessment, spatial variation analysis across monitoring stations, temporal pattern recognition capabilities, and comprehensive model validation through multiple evaluation metrics.

\textbf{Primary Algorithm Performance Assessment} The comprehensive evaluation of machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, and traditional time series methods established Extra Trees Regressor as the optimal solution for urban air quality prediction, achieving exceptional test performance with R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.7724, MAE of 5.96 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, and RMSE of 8.87 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, representing a substantial improvement over all other approaches including advanced deep learning architectures through its unique combination of randomized feature selection and bootstrap aggregation that effectively captures complex non-linear relationships inherent in atmospheric systems while maintaining robust generalization capability for the right-skewed distribution of NO\textsubscript{2} concentrations (0 to 407.81 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}). Random Forest emerged as the second-best performer with R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.7337, MAE of 6.38 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, and RMSE of 9.60 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, followed by Bagging Random Forest with R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.6962, while the best-performing deep learning model, Keras BiLSTM, achieved R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.6200, MAE of 7.90 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, and RMSE of 11.46 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, demonstrating that tree-based ensemble methods outperform sophisticated neural network architectures for this atmospheric prediction task, with the performance gap between Extra Trees and the top deep learning model representing a 24.7\% improvement in R\textsuperscript{2} and 24.6\% reduction in MAE, highlighting the effectiveness of ensemble diversity and variance reduction over complex neural architectures for urban air quality forecasting.

\textbf{Ensemble Method Superiority Analysis} The systematic evaluation revealed a clear hierarchy favoring ensemble approaches over individual algorithms, with bagging methods consistently outperforming boosting techniques in atmospheric prediction applications, challenging conventional wisdom where boosting algorithms like XGBoost often dominate, as evidenced by the Voting Regressor (combining Random Forest, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting through hard voting) achieving R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.6686 while XGBoost individually reached R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.6628, indicating that simple ensemble combination strategies may not always improve upon the best individual algorithm performance. Boosting algorithms showed moderate performance with XGBoost (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.6628), CatBoost (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.6547), and LightGBM (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.6014), with performance degradation potentially attributed to the sequential error correction approach being less suitable for the temporal autocorrelation and spatial heterogeneity present in atmospheric data, while the superior performance of bagging methods suggests that variance reduction through bootstrap aggregation is more effective than bias reduction through sequential learning for urban air quality prediction.

\textbf{Deep Learning Model Performance Analysis} The evaluation of deep learning architectures revealed that advanced neural network models, while sophisticated, did not surpass traditional ensemble methods for atmospheric prediction in this study, with Keras BiLSTM emerging as the top-performing deep learning approach (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.6200, MAE 7.90 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, RMSE 11.46 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}), demonstrating the effectiveness of bidirectional LSTM architecture in capturing temporal dependencies inherent in time-series air quality data. Among Keras-based models, the performance hierarchy showed BiLSTM $>$ Residual DNN (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.5987) $>$ Deep DNN (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.5982) $>$ Autoencoder (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.5976), with recurrent architectures generally outperforming feedforward networks, suggesting that the sequential nature of atmospheric data benefits from memory-based neural architectures, while PyTorch implementations (ResNet R\textsuperscript{2} 0.1291, MLP R\textsuperscript{2} -0.0021) showed inferior performance potentially due to different implementation approaches, hyperparameter settings, or architectural configurations. The moderate performance of deep learning models compared to ensemble methods indicates that while neural networks can capture complex patterns, the atmospheric prediction task in this study may benefit more from the variance reduction and feature randomization strategies employed by tree-based ensembles rather than the deep hierarchical representations learned by neural networks.

\textbf{Traditional Method Performance Limitations} Traditional machine learning approaches demonstrated significant limitations in capturing atmospheric complexity, with linear methods (Linear Regression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet) achieving R\textsuperscript{2} values between 0.1273 and 0.1566, indicating fundamental inadequacy for modeling the non-linear relationships between meteorological variables and NO\textsubscript{2} concentrations, while Support Vector Regression with RBF kernel achieved R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.3304, showing improved non-linear modeling capability but remaining substantially inferior to both ensemble methods and deep learning approaches. The Multi-Layer Perceptron achieved moderate performance (R\textsuperscript{2} 0.5010), suggesting that while neural networks can capture non-linear patterns, the relatively simple architecture and limited hyperparameter optimization may have constrained performance, and K-Nearest Neighbors achieved R\textsuperscript{2} of 0.5860, demonstrating the effectiveness of local pattern recognition but highlighting limitations in handling the high-dimensional feature space and temporal dependencies present in atmospheric data.

\textbf{Time Series Model Comparison} Traditional time series approaches showed poor performance, with all ARIMA variants achieving negative R\textsuperscript{2} values indicating worse performance than a simple mean predictor, as ARIMA(1,1,2) achieved the best time series performance with MAE of 13.39 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3} and R\textsuperscript{2} of -0.2652, while the naive forecasting approach resulted in R\textsuperscript{2} of -1.9944, demonstrating that traditional time series methods, which rely primarily on temporal patterns, are inadequate for atmospheric prediction where meteorological variables provide crucial predictive information.

\textbf{Station-Specific Performance Analysis} The spatial analysis across Cork's five monitoring locations reveals substantial heterogeneity in prediction accuracy, with University College Cork achieving the highest accuracy (MAE 4.82 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, R\textsuperscript{2} 0.83) representing an institutional environment with relatively stable atmospheric conditions and limited direct traffic influence, while Heatherton Park presented the most challenging prediction environment (MAE 6.92 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, R\textsuperscript{2} 0.70) reflecting complex urban background conditions with multiple emission sources and variable atmospheric mixing, with the performance difference representing a 43.8\% increase in MAE and 15.7\% decrease in R\textsuperscript{2} highlighting the importance of site-specific model calibration for operational deployment. South Link Road, despite being a high-traffic arterial location, achieved intermediate performance (MAE 5.96 $\mu$g/m\textsuperscript{3}, R\textsuperscript{2} 0.77), suggesting that consistent traffic patterns may actually facilitate prediction compared to more variable background conditions, indicating that predictable emission sources, even if intense, may be more amenable to machine learning approaches than diffuse or variable sources.

\textbf{Model Generalization and Overfitting Assessment} The systematic evaluation of training versus testing performance reveals critical insights into model generalization capabilities, with Extra Trees demonstrating controlled overfitting (training R² 1.0000 vs testing R² 0.7724, representing a manageable 0.2276 generalization gap) that maintains robust predictive capability while indicating acceptable model complexity for practical deployment, contrasting with Decision Tree's severe overfitting (training R² 1.0000 vs testing R² 0.3565, gap = 0.6435) that demonstrates the fundamental limitation of single trees and validates the necessity of ensemble approaches for atmospheric prediction. Traditional methods showed consistent underperformance rather than overfitting issues, with Linear Regression (R² 0.1566), Ridge (R² 0.1566), and Lasso (R² 0.1385) indicating inherent model inadequacy for capturing complex non-linear relationships, while Support Vector Regression (R² 0.3304) and MLP Regressor (R² 0.5010) achieved intermediate results with moderate overfitting tendencies, suggesting that deeper architectures or more sophisticated neural network designs might improve atmospheric prediction capabilities.

\textbf{Ensemble Algorithm Generalization Patterns} Ensemble algorithms demonstrated systematic advantages with varying generalization patterns that provide insights into optimal model selection strategies, with Random Forest showing a 0.27 generalization gap (training R² 0.96 vs testing R² 0.73) and Bagging RF exhibiting a 0.23 gap, confirming that bagging ensembles provide optimal balance between learning capacity and generalization through variance reduction via bootstrap aggregation, while boosting algorithms displayed different characteristics with XGBoost (gap = 0.14) and CatBoost (gap = 0.10) showing smaller generalization gaps indicating better control of overfitting through sequential learning and regularization mechanisms, though their lower absolute testing performance compared to bagging methods suggests that the bias-variance trade-off favors variance reduction over bias correction for atmospheric prediction applications. These findings have important implications for operational deployment, suggesting that while boosting algorithms may appear more stable based on generalization gaps alone, bagging ensembles provide superior predictive accuracy for atmospheric applications, with the controlled overfitting observed in top-performing models (Extra Trees, Random Forest) representing acceptable model complexity that captures atmospheric system complexity while maintaining practical utility.

\textbf{Feature Importance and Model Interpretability} The analysis of feature importance reveals critical insights into the drivers of urban air quality variation, with meteorological variables dominating the predictive hierarchy as temperature emerges as the most influential predictor (correlation coefficient -0.45) reflecting its fundamental role in atmospheric chemistry, photochemical reactions, and boundary layer dynamics, wind speed demonstrates the second-highest importance (correlation -0.32) confirming its critical role in pollutant dilution and transport through enhanced horizontal and vertical mixing, and relative humidity shows positive correlation (0.28) reflecting its complex role in atmospheric chemistry where higher humidity can promote secondary particle formation and affect pollutant removal processes. Temporal features exhibit significant predictive power, with hour-of-day showing strong correlations with traffic patterns and human activity cycles as the model successfully captures rush-hour peaks (morning 8-9 AM, evening 5-7 PM) and weekend variations, demonstrating its ability to learn human behavioral patterns that drive emission variations, while seasonal patterns are effectively captured through month and day-of-year features, enabling accurate prediction of heating season impacts and meteorological seasonal cycles.

\textbf{Operational Forecasting Capabilities and Uncertainty Quantification} The 1-year forecast visualization in Figure \ref{fig:no2_forecast_comprehensive} demonstrates the model's operational capability for long-term air quality prediction, providing essential information for urban planning and public health management, with the forecast showing seasonal patterns (predicted winter concentrations averaging 22.4 $\mu$g/m³ and summer levels at 16.8 $\mu$g/m³, representing a 33.3\% seasonal variation consistent with historical patterns) and monthly forecast ranges from 17.5 $\mu$g/m³ (July minimum) to 20.8 $\mu$g/m³ (January maximum), with an annual average prediction of 18.5 $\mu$g/m³ and forecast uncertainty bands indicating 95\% confidence intervals ranging from ±3.2 $\mu$g/m³ during stable summer conditions to ±5.8 $\mu$g/m³ during variable winter periods, providing quantitative uncertainty assessment essential for decision-making applications.

\textbf{Comparative Analysis with International Studies} The achieved performance (R² = 0.7724, MAE = 5.96 $\mu$g/m³) represents competitive accuracy compared to international air quality prediction studies, with comparison to similar European urban environments showing comparable or superior performance as studies in Madrid achieved R² = 0.68-0.72 while London-based research reported R² = 0.65-0.71 for NO\textsubscript{2} prediction, with the Cork study's superior performance potentially reflecting the comprehensive meteorological dataset, extended temporal coverage, and optimized ensemble methodology. The performance advantage over traditional time series methods (ARIMA models showing negative R² values) demonstrates the critical importance of incorporating meteorological variables in atmospheric prediction, aligning with international research emphasizing the limitations of purely temporal approaches for environmental forecasting applications.

\textbf{Practical Implications for Urban Air Quality Management} The comprehensive evaluation results support several important conclusions for atmospheric prediction applications and urban environmental management, with ensemble methods, particularly Extra Trees and Random Forest algorithms, consistently outperforming traditional machine learning approaches and time series methods in urban air quality forecasting through bagging techniques demonstrating superior performance compared to boosting algorithms in atmospheric applications, while the spatial performance variation across monitoring stations (R² ranging from 0.70 to 0.83) emphasizes the importance of site-specific model calibration and validation for operational deployment as the superior performance at institutional sites (University College Cork) compared to complex urban background locations (Heatherton Park) suggests that predictable emission patterns facilitate more accurate predictions than variable diffuse sources. The model's ability to capture multi-scale temporal patterns (diurnal, seasonal, inter-annual) demonstrates practical utility for both short-term air quality forecasting and long-term trend analysis, with successful prediction of traffic-related peaks and seasonal variations providing evidence for operational deployment in early warning systems and regulatory compliance monitoring, while these findings carry significant implications for real-world air quality forecasting systems, suggesting that Extra Trees-based models with comprehensive meteorological inputs serve as a reliable foundation for urban atmospheric prediction where the controlled overfitting observed in optimal models represents acceptable complexity for practical deployment, the ensemble approach provides robustness against individual algorithm limitations, and the consistent performance across multiple monitoring sites underscores model transferability while emphasizing the necessity of location-specific validation in practical deployments.

\section{Discussion \& Limitation}
\label{sec:discussion}

This study demonstrates the critical importance of meteorological and temporal features in predicting urban NO\textsubscript{2} concentrations through comprehensive analysis of 56,708 observations across five Cork monitoring locations. The analysis revealed key meteorological predictors (temperature: -0.45, relative humidity: 0.28) aligning with atmospheric chemistry principles, while temporal analysis showed pronounced diurnal and seasonal patterns corresponding to traffic patterns. Performance evaluation across 33 algorithms (17 machine learning, 11 deep learning, 5 time series) demonstrated ensemble method superiority, with Extra Trees achieving MAE 5.96 $\mu$g/m³ and R\textsuperscript{2} 0.7724, outperforming XGBoost (MAE 7.56, R\textsuperscript{2} 0.6628), the best deep learning model Keras BiLSTM (MAE 7.90, R\textsuperscript{2} 0.6200), and other algorithms. Notable findings include the superior performance of bagging ensemble methods (Extra Trees, Random Forest) over boosting algorithms, demonstrating the effectiveness of algorithmic diversity and ensemble regularization in atmospheric prediction applications. The study advanced atmospheric modeling through innovations in wind-adjusted concentrations (normalizing by wind speed plus 0.5 m/s), comprehensive outlier detection (addressing 1.1\% anomalous observations), and negative NO\textsubscript{2} value handling (establishing -2.0 $\mu$g/m³ lower bound). Regulatory benchmarking against WHO 2021 guidelines revealed frequent exceedances, demonstrating the utility of machine learning for early warning systems and pollution control planning.

Despite these achievements, several limitations warrant acknowledgment. The models operate under assumptions that may not fully capture atmospheric complexity, with temporal independence assumptions potentially violated in autocorrelated time series. Regional specificity to Cork limits broader applicability, while data quality constraints include instrumental precision limitations and the 75\% completeness criterion for annual averages. The feature selection process may have overlooked important variables, particularly chemical transformation processes and three-dimensional meteorological fields. Ensemble algorithms, while superior in performance, show operational limitations: Random Forest exhibited overfitting (training R\textsuperscript{2} 0.96 to testing R\textsuperscript{2} 0.73), while computational complexity and hyperparameter sensitivity pose challenges for real-time applications. Spatial-temporal resolution limitations from fixed monitoring stations, the 6-kilometer distance between city center and meteorological station, and COVID-19's impact on traffic patterns (2020-2023) introduce additional uncertainties. Future research directions should focus on multi-city modeling frameworks, integration of high-resolution emission data and satellite observations, implementation of adaptive learning algorithms, exploration of deep learning architectures (particularly RNNs and attention mechanisms), and development of explainable AI approaches to enhance interpretability while maintaining predictive performance. These advancements would address current limitations while supporting evidence-based environmental management and sustainable urban development.
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This comprehensive study has demonstrated the effectiveness of machine learning approaches for predicting urban NO\textsubscript{2} concentrations in Cork, Ireland, through analysis of 56,708 observations across five monitoring locations (2014-2023), revealing key meteorological predictors (temperature: -0.45, wind speed: -0.32, relative humidity: 0.28) alongside temporal features reflecting human activity patterns. Extra Trees emerged as the consistently optimal algorithm among all approaches including machine learning, deep learning, and time series methods, achieving MAE 5.96 $\mu$g/m³ and R\textsuperscript{2} 0.7724, demonstrating superior generalization capability while bagging ensemble methods outperformed both boosting algorithms and sophisticated deep learning architectures across the evaluation framework. The study advanced environmental prediction through methodological innovations including wind-adjusted concentration methodology, comprehensive outlier detection (addressing 1.1\% anomalous observations), and multi-metric evaluation with bootstrap resampling, while regulatory benchmarking against WHO 2021 guidelines revealed frequent exceedances requiring intervention. Future research should prioritize advanced architectures (RNNs, LSTMs, ARIMA, Prophet) and Bayesian approaches for uncertainty quantification \cite{saminathan2024pm25,wang2025high,ma2023multi}, while expanding scope through multi-city studies, satellite observations integration, and real-time adaptive learning systems. The exploration of alternative data sources (social media, mobile sensors, citizen science) combined with explainable AI techniques (SHAP values, feature attribution) and integration of chemical transport models with climate change projections would enhance both predictive capability and stakeholder acceptance, ultimately supporting evidence-based environmental management and sustainable urban development in an era of rapid urbanization and climate change.

title: Shortermism and excessive risk taking in optimal execution with a target performance
summary:
We deal with the optimal execution problem when the broker's goal is to reach
a performance barrier avoiding a downside barrier. The performance is provided
by the wealth accumulated by trading in the market, the shares detained by the
broker evaluated at the market price plus a slippage cost yielding a quadratic
inventory cost. Over a short horizon, this type of remuneration leads, at the
same time, to a more aggressive and less risky strategy compared to the
classical one, and over a long horizon the performance turns to be poorer and
more dispersed.

title: From General Relation Patterns to Task-Specific Decision-Making in Continual Multi-Agent Coordination
summary:
Continual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (Co-MARL) requires agents to
address catastrophic forgetting issues while learning new coordination policies
with the dynamics team. In this paper, we delve into the core of Co-MARL,
namely Relation Patterns, which refer to agents' general understanding of
interactions. In addition to generality, relation patterns exhibit
task-specificity when mapped to different action spaces. To this end, we
propose a novel method called General Relation Patterns-Guided Task-Specific
Decision-Maker (RPG). In RPG, agents extract relation patterns from dynamic
observation spaces using a relation capturer. These task-agnostic relation
patterns are then mapped to different action spaces via a task-specific
decision-maker generated by a conditional hypernetwork. To combat forgetting,
we further introduce regularization items on both the relation capturer and the
conditional hypernetwork. Results on SMAC and LBF demonstrate that RPG
effectively prevents catastrophic forgetting when learning new tasks and
achieves zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks.

title: Critical Point Processes Obtained from a Gaussian Random Field with a View Towards Statistics
summary:
This paper establishes the theoretical foundation for statistical
applications of an intriguing new type of spatial point processes called
critical point processes. These point processes, residing in Euclidean space,
consist of the critical points of latent smooth Gaussian random fields or of
subsets of critical points like minima, saddle points etc. Despite of the
simplicity of their definition, the mathematical analysis of critical point
processes is non-trivial involving for example deep results on the geometry of
random fields, Sobolev space theory, chaos expansions, and multiple
Wiener-It{\^o} integrals. We provide explicit expressions for fundamental
moment characteristics used in spatial point process statistics like the
intensity parameter, the pair correlation function, and higher order intensity
functions. The crucial dependence structure (attraction or repulsiveness) of a
critical point process is discussed in depth and is in particular related to
the dimension of the points and the type of critical points (extrema, saddle
points, or all of the critical points). We propose simulation strategies based
on spectral methods or smoothing of grid-based simulations and show that
resulting approximate critical point process simulations asymptotically
converge to the exact critical point process distribution. Finally, under the
increasing domain framework, we obtain asymptotic results for linear and
bilinear statistics of a critical point process. In particular, we obtain a
multivariate central limit theorem for the intensity parameter estimate and a
modified version of Ripley's K-function.

\begin{abstract}
This paper establishes the theoretical foundation for
statistical applications of an intriguing new type of spatial point
processes called critical point processes. These point processes,
residing in Euclidean space,  consist of the critical points of 
latent smooth Gaussian random fields or of subsets of critical points like minima, saddle
points etc.  Despite of the simplicity of their definition, the
mathematical analysis of critical point processes is non-trivial
involving for example deep results on the geometry of random fields,
Sobolev space theory, chaos expansions, and multiple Wiener-It{\^ o}
integrals.  We provide explicit expressions for fundamental moment
characteristics used in spatial point process statistics like the intensity
parameter, the pair correlation function, and higher order intensity
functions. The crucial dependence structure
(attraction or repulsiveness) of
a critical point process is discussed in depth and is in particular
related to the dimension of the points and the type of critical points
(extrema, saddle points, or all of the critical points). We propose
simulation strategies based on spectral methods or
smoothing of grid-based simulations and
show that resulting approximate critical point process simulations
asymptotically converge to  the exact critical point process
distribution. Finally, under the increasing domain framework, we
obtain asymptotic results for linear and bilinear statistics of a  critical point process. In particular, we obtain a multivariate central limit theorem for the intensity parameter estimate and a modified version of Ripley's $K$-function.
\end{abstract}
